_note: BC organisms added by the hack (Living Atlas schema plus bc_habitats, stage_index and invasive). Entries with "override": true replace a Living Atlas organism for this hack only. See docs/ROSTER.md.

species.name: Skunk Cabbage Seed
species.range: Swamps and wet forests of coastal BC
species.entry: Its seeds sit in a green, berry-like fruit on a thick stalk. They drop into the mud of the swamp where the parent grows.

species.name: Skunk Cabbage Shoot
species.range: Swamps and wet forests of coastal BC
species.entry: A young plant grows a rosette of leaves for several years before it is ready to bloom. Its roots hold tight in waterlogged mud.

species.name: Western Skunk Cabbage
species.range: Swamps and wet forests of coastal BC
species.entry: Its bright yellow hood blooms in early spring and smells like a skunk, drawing the beetles that pollinate it. Needle-like crystals in its leaves sting the mouths of plant-eaters.

species.name: Morel Spore
species.range: Burned forests of the BC Interior
species.entry: Morel spores drift on the wind by the billion. Most land nowhere useful, but a few settle into the ash of a fresh burn.

species.name: Morel Mycelium
species.range: Burned forests of the BC Interior
species.entry: Threads of mycelium spread through the soil under a burned forest. After a fire kills the trees around it, the fungus gets ready to fruit.

species.name: Burn Morel
species.range: Burned forests of the BC Interior
species.entry: Morels fruit in huge numbers in the spring after a forest fire. Their honeycomb caps push up through the ash among the blackened trunks.

species.name: Beaver Kit
species.range: Rivers, lakes and wetlands across BC
species.entry: Kits are born in spring inside the family lodge and can swim within a day. Their thick fur traps air that keeps them warm and afloat.

species.name: Yearling Beaver
species.range: Rivers, lakes and wetlands across BC
species.entry: Young beavers stay with their family for about two years. Yearlings help patch the dam and bring food for the newest kits.

species.name: Spirit Bear
species.range: Great Bear Rainforest, North Coast of BC
species.entry: A black bear with a white coat, caused by a rare gene. White bears catch salmon more often in daylight, perhaps because the fish see them less easily against the sky.

species.name: Glass Sponge Reef
species.range: Hecate Strait and the Strait of Georgia
species.entry: These reefs of glass sponges were thought to be extinct for 40 million years until they were found off BC in 1987. Some are about 9,000 years old.

species.name: Marbled Murrelet
species.range: Coast of BC and old-growth forests inland
species.entry: A seabird that nests high on mossy branches of old-growth trees, far from the sea. Its nest was a mystery until the first one was found in 1974.

species.name: Vancouver Island Marmot
species.range: Subalpine meadows of central Vancouver Island
species.entry: Found only on Vancouver Island, fewer than 30 lived in the wild in 2003. Marmots bred in zoos and released have helped it climb back.

species.name: Northern Spotted Owl
species.range: Old-growth forests of southwestern BC
species.entry: Only a handful of these owls remain in the wild in BC. The larger barred owl, which spread west over the last century, takes over its forests.

species.name: Marrella
species.range: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park
species.entry: The most common animal in the Burgess Shale, with more than 25,000 fossils found. It was the first one Charles Walcott split from the rock in 1909.

species.name: Phantom Orchid
species.range: Shady forests of southern Vancouver Island and the Fraser Valley
species.entry: A pure white orchid with no green at all. It takes its food from fungi in the soil and can stay underground for years before it blooms again.

species.name: Ogopogo
species.range: Okanagan Lake (reported)
species.entry: Reported in Okanagan Lake since the 1920s as a long animal with humps along its back. No body, bone or clear photo has ever been found.

species.name: Sasquatch
species.range: Coastal forests of BC (reported)
species.entry: Reported in BC forests as a tall, hairy walker on two legs. People have cast many large footprints in plaster, but no body or bone has ever been found.

species.name: Caddy
species.range: Salish Sea (reported)
species.entry: Named after Cadboro Bay near Victoria by a newspaper editor in 1933. Sailors describe a long serpent with a horse-like head, but none has ever been caught.

species.name: Wiwaxia
species.range: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park
species.entry: A small sea creature covered in overlapping scales with two rows of tall spines. It crept over the sea floor about 508 million years ago.

species.name: Sidneyia
species.range: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park
species.entry: One of the bigger hunters of the Burgess Shale sea. Fossils show bits of small shelled animals and trilobites in its gut.

species.name: Sockeye Alevin
species.range: Gravel beds of BC rivers such as the Adams
species.entry: Newly hatched sockeye hide in the river gravel and live off the yolk sac on their bellies. They come out once the yolk is used up.

species.name: Sockeye Smolt
species.range: Lakes and rivers of BC, heading to sea
species.entry: After a year or two in a lake, young sockeye turn silver and head for the sea. They remember the smell of home water to find their way back years later.

species.name: Sockeye Salmon
species.range: Rivers and lakes of BC, and the North Pacific
species.entry: Adults turn bright red with green heads as they swim upriver to spawn where they hatched. Their bodies then feed the bears, eagles and trees along the stream.

species.name: Tree Frog Tadpole
species.range: Ponds and wetlands across southern BC
species.entry: Pacific tree frog tadpoles graze algae in shallow ponds. They grow legs and leave the water a couple of months after hatching.

species.name: Pacific Tree Frog
species.range: Ponds, gardens and forests across southern BC
species.entry: This small frog can change from green to brown over a few weeks. Its loud spring chorus is the familiar "ribbit" heard in many films.

species.name: Western Toad Tadpole
species.range: Lakes and ponds across BC
species.entry: Western toad tadpoles gather in huge black swarms in warm shallows. Each summer, thousands of tiny toadlets leave some BC lakes at once.

species.name: Western Toad
species.range: Forests, meadows and wetlands across BC
species.entry: Glands behind its eyes ooze a bitter poison that makes predators drop it. It walks more than it hops and shelters in burrows.

species.name: Newt Larva
species.range: Ponds and lakes of coastal BC
species.entry: Rough-skinned newt larvae have feathery gills and hunt tiny animals in ponds. They lose their gills before leaving the water.

species.name: Rough-skinned Newt
species.range: Forests and ponds of coastal BC
species.entry: Its skin holds tetrodotoxin, one of the strongest poisons known. When threatened, it arches its back to flash a bright orange belly.

species.name: Crab Megalopa
species.range: Coastal waters of BC
species.entry: After months drifting in the plankton, young Dungeness crabs settle as megalopae. Huge swarms of them wash into BC bays in spring.

species.name: Dungeness Crab
species.range: Sandy and muddy bottoms of the BC coast
species.entry: It buries itself in sand with only its eyes showing. To grow, it sheds its whole shell and hides while the new one hardens.

species.name: Darner Nymph
species.range: Ponds and lakes across BC
species.entry: The nymph lives underwater for a year or more. It snaps prey with a hinged lower lip and jets away by squirting water from its rear.

species.name: Paddle-tailed Darner
species.range: Ponds, lakes and meadows across BC
species.entry: A large blue-spotted dragonfly that hunts other insects on the wing. It can fly forward, backward and hover in place.

species.name: Mourning Cloak Caterpillar
species.range: Willows and aspens across BC
species.entry: These spiny black caterpillars with red spots feed together in groups on willow and aspen leaves.

species.name: Mourning Cloak
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: It survives the winter as an adult, tucked under bark with an antifreeze in its body. It is often the first butterfly seen in spring, sometimes with snow still on the ground.

species.name: American Black Bear
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: The most common bear in BC, found in almost every forest. In autumn it can eat 20,000 calories a day to fatten up for winter.

species.name: Cougar
species.range: Forests and mountains across southern BC
species.entry: Vancouver Island has one of the densest cougar populations in the world. A cougar can leap more than 5 metres up into a tree.

species.name: Canada Lynx
species.range: Northern and mountain forests of BC
species.entry: Its huge furry paws work like snowshoes. Its numbers rise and fall every ten years or so along with the snowshoe hares it hunts.

species.name: Coyote
species.range: Across BC, including Vancouver
species.entry: Coyotes have moved into cities across BC, including Stanley Park. They eat almost anything, from mice and berries to garbage.

species.name: Moose
species.range: Forests and wetlands of central and northern BC
species.entry: The largest deer in the world. It wades into lakes for water plants and can dive almost 6 metres to reach them.

species.name: Roosevelt Elk
species.range: Vancouver Island and the Sunshine Coast
species.entry: The largest elk in North America. In autumn the bulls bugle and clash antlers to win a group of females.

species.name: Black-tailed Deer
species.range: Coastal forests and gardens of BC
species.entry: A coastal kind of mule deer with a black tail. Fawns have white spots and lie still in the grass while their mother feeds.

species.name: Mountain Caribou
species.range: Inland rainforests and mountains of eastern BC
species.entry: In winter it walks on deep, hard snowpack to reach lichens hanging from old trees. Both males and females grow antlers.

species.name: American Pika
species.range: Rocky slopes in the BC mountains
species.entry: A small relative of rabbits that lives in rock piles. All summer it gathers grass and flowers into hay piles to eat through the winter.

species.name: Hoary Marmot
species.range: Alpine meadows of BC mountains
species.entry: Its shrill alarm whistle gave the town of Whistler its name. It hibernates for up to eight months of the year.

species.name: Douglas Squirrel
species.range: Coastal conifer forests of BC
species.entry: It cuts green cones from the treetops and buries thousands of them in piles for winter. The cones it forgets can sprout into new trees.

species.name: Northern Flying Squirrel
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: It glides between trees on flaps of skin at night. It eats truffles and spreads their spores, which help the trees grow.

species.name: North American Porcupine
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: About 30,000 quills cover its back. They come loose at a touch, and their tiny barbs work them deeper into an attacker.

species.name: North American River Otter
species.range: Rivers, lakes and seashores across BC
species.entry: It closes its ears and nostrils underwater. River otters often hunt along BC beaches and are mistaken for sea otters.

species.name: American Mink
species.range: Streams, marshes and shores across BC
species.entry: A small, fierce hunter of fish, frogs and crabs. Like a skunk, it can spray a strong-smelling musk.

species.name: Pacific Marten
species.range: Coastal and mountain forests of BC
species.entry: It races through the treetops after squirrels. In winter it hunts voles in tunnels under the snow.

species.name: Fisher
species.range: Forests of central and northern BC
species.entry: One of the few predators that can safely hunt porcupines. Its ankles turn so far that it can climb down trees head first.

species.name: American Badger
species.range: Grasslands of the BC Interior
species.entry: It digs faster than almost any animal, chasing ground squirrels right through their burrows. Only a few hundred live in BC.

species.name: Little Brown Bat
species.range: Caves, attics and forests across BC
species.entry: It finds insects in the dark by their echoes and can catch hundreds of small insects in an hour. White-nose syndrome now threatens it.

species.name: Snowshoe Hare
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: Its coat turns from brown in summer to white in winter. Its big hind feet keep it from sinking in snow.

species.name: Coast Mole
species.range: Fields and gardens of the Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley
species.entry: It swims through soil with huge shovel-like hands. The molehills in BC lawns are the dirt it pushes up from its tunnels.

species.name: Bushy-tailed Woodrat
species.range: Rocky cliffs, caves and old buildings across BC
species.entry: This pack rat collects shiny objects for its nest and sometimes leaves a stick or stone in their place. Its nests can be used for thousands of years.

species.name: Mountain Beaver
species.range: Wet forests of the southern Coast Mountains
species.entry: Not a beaver at all, it is the last living species of a very old family of rodents. It eats ferns that most animals avoid.

species.name: Sea Otter
species.range: West coast of Vancouver Island and the Central Coast
species.entry: It cracks urchins on a rock balanced on its chest. By eating urchins, it lets kelp forests grow back.

species.name: Steller Sea Lion
species.range: Rocky islands along the BC coast
species.entry: The largest sea lion in the world. Males roar from rocky islands to guard their group of females.

species.name: Harbour Seal
species.range: Harbours and bays along the whole BC coast
species.entry: The most common marine mammal in BC. Its whiskers feel the wakes of fish swimming by, even in dark water.

species.name: Dall's Porpoise
species.range: Deep waters along the BC coast
species.entry: One of the fastest small whales. It throws up a "rooster tail" of spray as it races along the surface.

species.name: Pacific White-sided Dolphin
species.range: Coastal waters and inlets of BC
species.entry: It travels in noisy pods that can number in the hundreds. It often leaps and somersaults beside boats.

species.name: Steller's Jay
species.range: Forests and towns across BC
species.entry: BC's provincial bird. It mimics the scream of a red-tailed hawk to scare other birds away from food.

species.name: Rufous Hummingbird
species.range: Meadows and forest edges across BC
species.entry: For its size, it makes one of the longest migrations of any bird, from Mexico to BC. Males fiercely chase other birds from their flowers.

species.name: Anna's Hummingbird
species.range: Gardens of southern BC, all year
species.entry: Males dive from high in the sky and make a loud chirp with their tail feathers. On cold nights it lowers its body heat to save energy.

species.name: Great Blue Heron
species.range: Shores and wetlands of the BC coast
species.entry: It stands perfectly still in shallow water, then spears fish with its long bill. One of the largest colonies nests in Stanley Park.

species.name: Sandhill Crane
species.range: Wetlands and bogs of BC, including Burns Bog
species.entry: Pairs dance together with leaps, bows and wing-flaps. They often paint their grey feathers rusty brown with muddy water.

species.name: Trumpeter Swan
species.range: Lakes, rivers and farm fields of BC in winter
species.entry: The heaviest flying bird in North America. It nearly died out in the 1930s, and many now spend the winter in BC.

species.name: Snow Goose
species.range: Fraser River delta in autumn and spring
species.entry: Tens of thousands stop on the Fraser delta each year on their way from Wrangel Island in Russia. They grub up marsh roots with their strong bills.

species.name: Harlequin Duck
species.range: Mountain rivers in summer and rocky coasts in winter
species.entry: It dives in fast white-water rivers to catch insects on the bottom. The males look painted with white stripes and chestnut sides.

species.name: Osprey
species.range: Lakes, rivers and coasts across BC
species.entry: It hovers, then plunges feet first to grab fish. It carries them head forward to cut through the air.

species.name: American Crow
species.range: Towns, farms and shores across BC
species.entry: Crows remember the faces of people who threaten them for years. Every evening thousands fly to one roost in Burnaby.

species.name: Varied Thrush
species.range: Wet coastal and mountain forests of BC
species.entry: Its song is a single long, buzzy whistle that echoes through foggy forests. It flips dead leaves to find insects and worms.

species.name: American Dipper
species.range: Fast mountain streams across BC
species.entry: A songbird that walks underwater along stream bottoms, gripping rocks to hunt insect larvae. It bobs up and down on rocks between dives.

species.name: Pileated Woodpecker
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: It chisels big rectangular holes in trees to reach carpenter ants. Owls, ducks and squirrels later nest in its old holes.

species.name: Northern Flicker
species.range: Open forests, farms and towns across BC
species.entry: A woodpecker that often feeds on the ground, lapping up ants with its long sticky tongue. Western birds flash salmon-red under their wings.

species.name: Bushtit
species.range: Gardens and shrubs of southern BC
species.entry: Tiny grey birds that move in chattering flocks. They weave a hanging nest like a long sock out of spider silk and moss.

species.name: Black-capped Chickadee
species.range: Forests and towns across BC
species.entry: On cold nights it lets its body cool to save energy. It hides thousands of seeds in autumn and remembers where they are.

species.name: Western Sandpiper
species.range: Roberts Bank and the Fraser delta in migration
species.entry: Huge flocks stop on the Fraser delta mudflats each spring. They sip the slimy film of microbes on the mud with brush-tipped tongues.

species.name: Rhinoceros Auklet
species.range: Nesting islands along the BC coast
species.entry: It grows a small horn on its bill each breeding season. It digs nest burrows on islands and comes back to them only after dark.

species.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
species.range: Alpine tundra of the BC mountains
species.entry: It turns pure white in winter and speckled grey-brown in summer to match the rocks. Feathers on its feet act as snowshoes.

species.name: Burrowing Owl
species.range: Grasslands of the southern BC Interior
species.entry: It nests underground in old badger and ground squirrel burrows. Its young hiss like a rattlesnake to scare off intruders.

species.name: Barred Owl
species.range: Forests across BC (spread west in the 1900s)
species.entry: It spread west across Canada in the last century and now lives all over BC. It eats almost anything and pushes out the spotted owl.

species.name: Belted Kingfisher
species.range: Rivers, lakes and shores across BC
species.entry: It dives headfirst for fish from a perch over the water. It nests at the end of a long tunnel it digs into a riverbank.

species.name: Sooty Grouse
species.range: Coastal mountain forests of BC
species.entry: In winter it lives high in conifers eating needles. In spring the males hoot so deeply that the sound is hard to trace.

species.name: Western Rattlesnake
species.range: Dry valleys of the southern BC Interior
species.entry: The only rattlesnake in BC. Pits on its face sense the body heat of mice in the dark, and it rattles its tail to warn larger animals.

species.name: Northern Rubber Boa
species.range: Forests and grasslands of southern BC
species.entry: Its blunt tail looks like a second head. When attacked it hides its real head and waves its tail instead.

species.name: Common Garter Snake
species.range: Wetlands, fields and gardens across BC
species.entry: Some garter snakes can eat rough-skinned newts that would kill almost any other predator. Their bodies resist the newt's poison.

species.name: Northern Alligator Lizard
species.range: Rocky clearings of southern BC
species.entry: If grabbed, it can drop its tail to escape. The tail keeps wriggling to distract the attacker while the lizard runs.

species.name: Western Painted Turtle
species.range: Ponds and lakes of southern BC
species.entry: BC's only native freshwater turtle. Its bright red-and-yellow belly is hidden until it climbs onto a log to bask.

species.name: Coastal Tailed Frog
species.range: Cold mountain streams of coastal BC
species.entry: One of the oldest frog lineages on Earth. Its tadpoles cling to rocks in fast streams with a sucker-like mouth.

species.name: Coastal Giant Salamander
species.range: Streams of the Chilliwack River valley
species.entry: One of the largest land salamanders in North America. It can bark like a small dog and bite hard when handled.

species.name: Ensatina
species.range: Moist forests of southwestern BC
species.entry: It has no lungs and breathes through its damp skin. When threatened it raises its tail, which oozes a sticky, bad-tasting milk.

species.name: American Bullfrog
species.range: Ponds of southern BC (introduced)
species.entry: Brought to BC for frog farms, it escaped and spread. It swallows almost anything it can fit in its mouth, including native frogs.

species.name: Chinook Salmon
species.range: Rivers of BC and the North Pacific
species.entry: The largest Pacific salmon. Southern resident orcas depend on chinook more than any other food.

species.name: Pink Salmon
species.range: Rivers of the BC coast
species.entry: The most numerous Pacific salmon. Spawning males grow a big hump on their backs, and every pink salmon lives exactly two years.

species.name: Steelhead
species.range: Rivers of BC and the North Pacific
species.entry: A rainbow trout that goes to sea and comes back big. Unlike most Pacific salmon, it can spawn and return to sea more than once.

species.name: White Sturgeon
species.range: The Fraser, Columbia and Nechako rivers
species.entry: The largest freshwater fish in North America, it can live over 100 years. Rows of bony plates have armoured its kind since the age of dinosaurs.

species.name: Eulachon
species.range: Rivers of the BC coast, including the Fraser
species.entry: This small smelt is so full of oil that a dried one will burn like a candle. Its spring runs feed eagles, sea lions and gulls.

species.name: Pacific Herring
species.range: Coastal waters of BC
species.entry: Each spring, herring spawn turns whole BC bays milky white. Their eggs stick to eelgrass and kelp and feed huge numbers of birds and whales.

species.name: Lingcod
species.range: Rocky reefs along the BC coast
species.entry: A big-mouthed hunter that waits on rocky reefs. Males guard the egg masses for weeks, and some have blue-green flesh.

species.name: Wolf Eel
species.range: Rocky reefs and dens along the BC coast
species.entry: Not a true eel, it crushes crabs and urchins with powerful jaws. Pairs share one den and may stay together for life.

species.name: Pacific Spiny Lumpsucker
species.range: Shallow kelp beds of the BC coast
species.entry: A round fish about the size of a golf ball. Its fins form a sucker on its belly that holds it to rocks and kelp.

species.name: Spotted Ratfish
species.range: Deep and shallow waters of the BC coast
species.entry: A relative of sharks from a very old family. It glides on wing-like fins and has a venomous spine in front of its back fin.

species.name: Bluntnose Sixgill Shark
species.range: Deep water of the Strait of Georgia
species.entry: A huge shark from an ancient family with six gill slits instead of five. It rises from the deep at night, and divers sometimes meet it near Hornby Island.

species.name: Pacific Lamprey
species.range: Rivers of BC and the North Pacific
species.entry: It has a round sucking mouth full of teeth instead of jaws. Adults feed on the blood of fish at sea, then climb waterfalls with their mouths to spawn.

species.name: Threespine Stickleback
species.range: Streams, lakes and shores across BC
species.entry: Males build nests of plants glued with a body thread and turn red-throated to court females. Some BC lakes hold their own species found nowhere else.

species.name: Sunflower Sea Star
species.range: Rocky reefs along the BC coast
species.entry: It can grow over 20 arms and speed over the sea floor on thousands of tube feet. A wasting disease since 2013 has wiped out most of them.

species.name: Ochre Sea Star
species.range: Rocky shores along the BC coast
species.entry: It pushes its stomach out into a mussel shell to digest it. Without it, mussels would cover the shore and crowd out everything else.

species.name: Purple Sea Urchin
species.range: Rocky coasts of western Vancouver Island
species.entry: It scrapes holes in solid rock with its teeth and spines. Without sea otters, urchins can eat a kelp forest down to bare rock.

species.name: Northern Abalone
species.range: Rocky shores along the BC coast
species.entry: A sea snail with a shell lined in rainbow mother-of-pearl. Harvesting it has been closed in BC since 1990 to help it recover.

species.name: Geoduck
species.range: Sandy bottoms of the BC coast
species.entry: The largest burrowing clam in the world, with a neck up to a metre long. Some geoducks live more than 160 years.

species.name: Opalescent Nudibranch
species.range: Docks and tide pools of the BC coast
species.entry: This sea slug eats hydroids and keeps their stinging cells in the tips of its own body for defence.

species.name: Lewis's Moon Snail
species.range: Sandy shores of the BC coast
species.entry: It drills a neat round hole in clam shells with its tongue and acid. Its eggs are laid in a sandy collar that washes up on BC beaches.

species.name: Spot Prawn
species.range: Deep rocky waters of the BC coast
species.entry: Every spot prawn starts life as a male and turns female at about two years old. It escapes by flicking its tail to shoot backward.

species.name: Plumose Anemone
species.range: Docks and rocky walls along the BC coast
species.entry: Tall white anemones that can reach a metre high. They catch plankton with feathery stinging tentacles and clone themselves by splitting.

species.name: Bull Kelp
species.range: Rocky coasts across BC
species.entry: It can grow 25 cm in a day and reach the surface in one summer. A gas-filled bulb holds its blades up in the sunlight.

species.name: Eelgrass
species.range: Sheltered bays of the BC coast
species.entry: A flowering plant that lives fully underwater. Its meadows shelter young salmon and herring and hold the sand in place.

species.name: European Green Crab
species.range: Bays of western Vancouver Island (introduced)
species.entry: An invader from Europe that reached BC in the late 1990s. It cuts down eelgrass and eats young clams and crabs.

species.name: Mountain Pine Beetle
species.range: Pine forests of the BC Interior
species.entry: An outbreak from the late 1990s killed more than half of the pine in BC. The beetles carry a blue-staining fungus into the trees.

species.name: Fire-chaser Beetle
species.range: Burned forests across BC
species.entry: Pits on its body sense the heat of a forest fire from far away. It flies toward the smoke to lay eggs in freshly burned trees.

species.name: Western Bumble Bee
species.range: Meadows and gardens across BC
species.entry: It shakes pollen loose from flowers by buzzing its flight muscles. Once common in BC, it has become much rarer.

species.name: Ten-lined June Beetle
species.range: Sandy soils of southern BC
species.entry: This striped beetle hisses by squeezing air out of its body when picked up. Its grubs live underground for up to four years.

species.name: Pacific Dampwood Termite
species.range: Rotting logs of coastal BC forests
species.entry: It lives inside damp, rotting logs and digests wood with microbes in its gut. Winged swarms fly out on warm autumn evenings.

species.name: Yellow-spotted Millipede
species.range: Forest floors of coastal BC
species.entry: When disturbed it oozes cyanide, which smells like almonds. Its bright yellow spots warn predators away.

species.name: Common Water Strider
species.range: Streams and ponds across BC
species.entry: Hairs on its legs let it stand on the surface of water. It feels ripples to find insects that fall in.

species.name: Western Thatching Ant
species.range: Grasslands and open forests of the BC Interior
species.entry: It builds big mounds of plant thatch over its nest that catch the sun and keep it warm. It sprays formic acid at intruders.

species.name: Douglas-fir
species.range: Coastal and Interior forests of BC
species.entry: Old Douglas-firs grow bark up to 30 cm thick that shields them from fire. Big Lonely Doug, near Port Renfrew, is about 66 metres tall.

species.name: Western Redcedar
species.range: Wet forests of coastal BC and the Interior wet belt
species.entry: BC's provincial tree. Natural chemicals in its wood resist rot, so fallen cedars last for centuries on the forest floor.

species.name: Sitka Spruce
species.range: Foggy coasts of BC, including the Carmanah Valley
species.entry: It grows only near the coast, where fog drips from its needles to water it. The Carmanah Giant, at about 95 metres, is the tallest tree in Canada.

species.name: Arbutus
species.range: Rocky coasts of southern Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands
species.entry: Canada's only native broadleaf evergreen tree. Its red-brown bark peels away in thin curls to show smooth green wood beneath.

species.name: Garry Oak
species.range: Southeastern Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands
species.entry: BC's only native oak. Its meadows bloom with blue camas in spring and are among the rarest habitats in Canada.

species.name: Lodgepole Pine
species.range: Forests of the BC Interior
species.entry: Many of its cones stay sealed with resin until a fire melts it open. Then seeds rain onto the ash, and a new forest starts.

species.name: Devil's Club
species.range: Wet forests across BC
species.entry: Sharp spines cover its stems and even the undersides of its huge leaves. It grows in thick patches along wet forest streams.

species.name: Salal
species.range: Coastal forests of BC
species.entry: This shrub forms thickets so dense that early explorers struggled through them. Bears and birds eat its dark purple berries.

species.name: Fireweed
species.range: Burns, clearings and roadsides across BC
species.entry: One of the first plants to bloom on burned ground, covering it in tall pink spikes. Each plant releases tens of thousands of fluffy seeds.

species.name: Round-leaved Sundew
species.range: Bogs across BC, including Burns Bog
species.entry: Its leaves are covered with glistening sticky hairs that trap insects. The plant digests them to get nutrients missing from the bog.

species.name: Sphagnum Moss
species.range: Bogs across BC, including Burns Bog
species.entry: It soaks up many times its own weight in water. Over thousands of years, it builds the peat that makes up bogs like Burns Bog.

species.name: Big Sagebrush
species.range: Dry valleys of the southern BC Interior
species.entry: Its silvery leaves are full of strong-smelling oils that keep most grazers away. Its long roots reach water deep under dry ground.

species.name: Brittle Prickly-pear
species.range: Dry slopes of the BC Interior and the Gulf Islands
species.entry: Yes, BC has a native cactus. Its small pads break off easily and stick to passing animals, then root wherever they fall.

species.name: Pacific Golden Chanterelle
species.range: Coastal forests of BC
species.entry: It grows with Douglas-fir and hemlock, trading nutrients from the soil for sugar from the trees' roots. It is one of the most-picked wild mushrooms in BC.

species.name: Lobster Mushroom
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: Not one mushroom but two: a red mould takes over another mushroom and reshapes it. The result looks and smells a little like cooked lobster.

species.name: Lungwort Lichen
species.range: Old-growth forests across BC
species.entry: A partnership of a fungus, a green alga and a cyanobacterium. It pulls nitrogen from the air that feeds the whole forest when it falls.

species.name: Honey Mushroom
species.range: Forests across BC
species.entry: Its underground threads can spread over many hectares, making it one of the largest living things on Earth. Wood it decays sometimes glows faintly at night.

species.name: Himalayan Blackberry
species.range: Roadsides and fields of southern BC (introduced)
species.entry: An invader that forms thorny walls across ditches and parks. Its arching canes root wherever their tips touch the ground.

species.name: Japanese Knotweed
species.range: Streamsides and towns of southern BC (introduced)
species.entry: Its roots can push through pavement and building foundations. A tiny piece of root can grow into a whole new patch.

species.name: Scotch Broom
species.range: Meadows and roadsides of southern BC (introduced)
species.entry: Brought from Europe as a garden plant in the 1850s, it now crowds out Garry oak meadows. Its seed pods pop in summer heat and fling seeds metres away.

species.name: American Beaver
species.range: Across North America
species.entry: It builds dams that turn streams into ponds, creating wetlands for many other animals. Its front teeth are orange because they are hardened with iron, and they never stop growing.

species.name: Opabinia
species.range: Cambrian, 508 million years ago · Burgess Shale, Canada
species.entry: It had five eyes on stalks and a long, flexible nozzle with a claw at the end. When it was first presented at a scientific meeting, the audience laughed, thinking it was a joke.

species.name: Pikaia
species.range: Cambrian, 508 million years ago · Burgess Shale, Canada
species.entry: This small, eel-like swimmer had a flexible rod along its back, the same feature that became the backbone in fish and people. It is one of the earliest known relatives of animals with backbones.
